title: Generous with money
hookLine: four parts and not one labeled give: the puzzle, and where giving really sits
tomorrow: borrowing money: a trap to stay out of, or sometimes a tool?

cards: Budgeting apps hand you neat little categories: rent, food, fun, savings. The Sigalovada hands you four parts. Read them again and something is strange.
Live on one. Put two to work. Keep one back.

None of them says give. A teaching that careful about a young man's money, and silent on sharing it? On a path where generosity, dana, opens the list of the ten perfections, that's a puzzle worth a few minutes.

teach.b: The answer sits in another sutta, spoken to the merchant Anathapindika. There the Buddha does the accounting a different way. Wealth gathered by effort, rightly earned, has four worthy uses.
First, make yourself happy with it, and your parents, your partner and children, your workers and your friends.
Second, protect it against loss: fire, water, thieves. Third, make offerings: to relatives, to guests, to those who have died, to the king, to the gods.
Fourth, give to the wandering holy people who live well and keep their minds clear. Look at that list for a second. Living, protecting, and then two kinds of giving.
So one way to solve the puzzle: giving isn't a fifth pile that only appears once the other four are full. It runs through the part you live on.
In the suttas, using money well already includes sharing it: a guest fed, a friend helped, a grandparent who has died remembered with an offering.

Notice too who comes first on the list: the people closest to you, and you yourself. Generosity here doesn't start by emptying your own table. A short collection called the Itivuttaka puts it more starkly.
If people knew what the Buddha knew about giving and sharing, it says, they wouldn't eat without sharing, not even their last mouthful.
A part given, then, isn't leftovers. It's how a householder lives, starting at their own table and moving outward, to the guest, the neighbor, the stranger.

how: Buddhist householders often give dana as food or money to monasteries and temples, and many also give to family, guests and people in need; some set aside a regular share of their income for it.

o: giving away everything you own to follow a teacher
giving as part of how you use what you earn
giving only once your savings are completely full

games.q: four worthy uses of wealth — tap the pairs.
p: your family, workers and friends made happy
offerings to relatives, guests, the dead
gifts to holy people who live well

s: in the suttas, you give only after the other parts are full
in the sutta to Anathapindika, sharing is part of using wealth well, not leftovers.
the Itivuttaka says people who understood giving wouldn't eat without sharing
the Sigalovada's four parts include one labeled giving
they don't: live on one, two to work, one kept back. that gap is today's puzzle.

games.q: your roommate says she'll start giving once she has real savings, maybe in ten years. using the sutta to Anathapindika, what's a fair reply?
o: fair enough: the suttas say to give only from surplus.
giving is for monks; householders are meant to build wealth first.
sharing is one of the worthy uses of wealth now, even in small amounts.
games.why: the sutta lists making friends and family happy, offerings and gifts among the uses of wealth rightly earned, not as a reward for later.

practice: Rest one hand open, palm up, on your knee. Bring to mind one person or place that could use a small gift: a friend short this month, a food bank, a temple roof.
Choose an amount small enough to feel easy, and let the open hand hold that choice for the rest of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Generous with money: dana with what you earn. Not a pile for later, but a thread through the part you live on.

orig.note: Pali and Sanskrit: giving, generosity; the first of the ten perfections.

carryVoice: Pocket this: a part given, woven into the part you live on. Three of five.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 4.61 (Pattakamma Sutta, to Anathapindika: four worthy deeds with wealth rightly earned: making self, parents, family, workers and friends happy; protecting it against fire, water, kings, thieves and heirs; the five offerings to relatives, guests, the departed, the king and the devas; gifts to ascetics and brahmins)
Itivuttaka 26 (if beings knew the result of giving and sharing, they would not eat without sharing, even their last mouthful)
